lead: Water in a kettle, LPG in a cylinder, steam entering a turbine: each is a pure fluid whose state is fixed by pressure P, molar volume V and temperature T. Plot every equilibrium state and you get a surface. Its three flat views — P–V, P–T and T–V — are the phase diagrams. They tell you which phase exists, where two phases coexist, and where boiling stops being possible at all. Power plants, refineries and refrigerant selection all begin by reading these diagrams, and every equation of state is drawn on them.
prereq: You need: Unit 1 — system, state, intensive and extensive variables, and the meaning of a pure substance.

sections.h3: The P-V-T surface and its three views

blocks.text: A pure fluid has one chemical species. In equilibrium its state is fixed by any two of P (pressure, in Pa or bar), T (temperature, in K) and V (molar volume, in m³/mol). The third follows.
Plot all such states with P up, V to the right and T going back. The sheet you get is the P-V-T surface.

Cut the surface three ways. At constant T you get a P–V isotherm. At constant P you get a T–V isobar. At constant V you get a P–T isochore. Each cut is a flat drawing that loses one variable but keeps every phase boundary.

Each view answers a different question. P–V answers work questions, because work is ∫P dV. P–T answers stability questions: which phase exists. T–V answers density questions: how much the volume changes on heating.
For water at 1 bar the two ends of the two-phase region are v_f = 0.001043 m³/kg (saturated liquid) and v_g = 1.694 m³/kg (saturated vapour).

Below the critical temperature a P–V isotherm has three parts. The left branch rises almost vertically: liquid hardly compresses. The right branch falls gently: vapour does compress. Between them the isotherm is horizontal at one pressure, the vapour pressure P<sup>sat</sup>(T).

The flat part is the two-phase region. Its left end is saturated liquid, the last liquid before a bubble of vapour appears. Its right end is saturated vapour, the last vapour before a drop of liquid appears. The horizontal length is v_g − v_f.

Repeat for every temperature below the critical temperature T_c. The left ends trace the saturated-liquid curve, the right ends the saturated-vapour curve. Together they close the saturation dome, also called the vapour dome. Inside the dome liquid and vapour coexist at the same P and T but at different V. A mixture of quality x has V = (1 − x)v_f + x·v_g, where x is the mass fraction of vapour and v_f and v_g are the saturated-liquid and saturated-vapour volumes.

The two curves meet at the critical point: for water, T_c = 374 °C and P_c = 221 bar. There saturated liquid and saturated vapour are identical, the latent heat is zero, and the meniscus between them disappears.

sections.h3: The P-T phase diagram and the phase rule

blocks.text: The P–T diagram is the most-used view. Three curves split the plane into solid, liquid and vapour regions. The sublimation curve separates solid from vapour. The fusion curve separates solid from liquid. The vaporisation curve separates liquid from vapour and ends at the critical point. All three meet at the triple point: for water, 0.01 °C and 0.00611 bar, where ice, liquid water and steam coexist.
For water the fusion curve leans left, so ice melts when the pressure rises. That is unusual; for most substances the fusion curve leans right.

Above the critical point the liquid and vapour regions merge. The fluid there is supercritical — neither liquid nor gas. No amount of pressure liquefies it while T stays above T_c. Supercritical carbon dioxide is used to strip caffeine from coffee beans, and dense supercritical water is studied as a reaction medium.

blocks.where: F is the number of intensive variables you may fix freely (degrees of freedom); C = 1 is the number of components; P_ph is the number of phases present. P on its own always means pressure, in bar or Pa.

blocks.text: One phase gives F = 2: choose T and P independently. Two phases give F = 1: choosing T fixes P = P<sup>sat</sup>(T). Three phases give F = 0: the triple point is one single state.

sections.h3: Mathematical representation: the equation of state

blocks.text: An equation of state is an algebraic relation among P, V and T for a fluid: f(P, V, T) = 0, or P = f(V, T). Every curve in the diagrams above is a solution of it. Some syllabi call this whole topic volumetric properties of pure fluids.
The simplest relation is the ideal gas law, PV = RT, where R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) is the gas constant. It holds when molecules are far apart; the next chapter develops it.

Real fluids need corrections. The compressibility factor Z = PV/RT measures the departure from ideal behaviour: Z = 1 for an ideal gas, Z < 1 when attraction between molecules pulls them together, and Z > 1 when their own size pushes them apart (high pressure). Virial equations add terms in 1/V. Cubic equations such as van der Waals carry two constants, a for attraction and b for molecular size, and can reproduce the dome and the critical point — see virial and cubic equations and compressibility factor.

Only a few universities go further and build the equation of state from the intermolecular potential energy u(r) between a pair of molecules. That step is statistical mechanics, not thermodynamics. Mixtures belong to Unit 6, fugacity to Unit 5, and property tables with the Clapeyron equation to Unit 4.

figure.caption: Pressure is plotted on a log scale, so the triple point and the 1 bar crossing are both visible. The curve from the triple point (0.00611 bar, 0.01 °C) to the critical point (221 bar, 374 °C) is the vaporisation curve. The line at 1 bar crosses it at about 100 °C, so 25 °C is liquid, 100 °C is liquid–vapour and 120 °C is vapour.

spec.aria: A pressure–temperature plot for water drawn with pressure on a log scale: the saturation curve runs from the triple point at 0.006 bar and 0.01 °C to the critical point at 221 bar and 374 °C, and a vertical line at 1 bar passes through 25 °C liquid, 100 °C boiling and 120 °C vapour.

examples.question: Water is held at 1 bar (100 kPa). (a) Name the phase at 25 °C, at 100 °C and at 120 °C. (b) Treat the vapour at 120 °C and 1 bar as ideal and estimate its specific volume. Data: R = 8.314 J/(mol·K), M = 18.015 g/mol.
steps: At 1 bar the saturation temperature of water is 99.6 °C, close enough to call 100 °C for this example. The normal boiling point, 100 °C, is at 1 atm = 1.01325 bar, slightly above 1 bar.
25 °C is below the saturation temperature. The fluid is a compressed (subcooled) liquid. One phase, F = 2.
100 °C equals the saturation temperature. Liquid and vapour coexist; any quality 0 ≤ x ≤ 1 is possible. Two phases, F = 1, so P alone fixes T.
120 °C is above the saturation temperature. The fluid is superheated vapour. One phase, F = 2.
Specific gas constant: R_s = R/M = 8.314/0.018015 = 461.5 J/(kg·K).
Ideal gas law per unit mass: v = R_s·T/P = 461.5 × 393.15/100 000 = 1.8144 m³/kg.
examples.answer: Liquid at 25 °C, liquid–vapour at 100 °C and vapour at 120 °C; the ideal-gas specific volume at 120 °C and 1 bar is 1.8144 m³/kg.

examples.question: Find the molar volume of water vapour at 1 bar and 120 °C, assuming ideal gas behaviour. Use R = 8.314 J/(mol·K).
steps: Ideal gas law in molar form: V = RT/P.
examples.answer: The molar volume is 0.03269 m³/mol, that is 32.69 L/mol.

traps: Reading the saturation curve as a single phase. On a P–T diagram every point of the vaporisation curve is a two-phase state: saturated liquid and saturated vapour together. On a P–V diagram the two branches of the dome are saturated liquid and saturated vapour, and only points strictly inside the dome are two-phase mixtures.
Calling the critical point a boiling point. At the critical point liquid and vapour are one phase and the latent heat is zero.
Thinking a gas above T_c can be liquefied by pressure alone. It cannot; you must first cool it below T_c.
Putting °C into PV = RT or any ideal-gas formula. Always convert to K.
Mixing molar or specific volume v with total volume V_total = n·v. Phase diagrams use volume per mole or per kilogram.

quiz.q: Define the triple point and give its value for water.
quiz.a: The single pressure and temperature at which solid, liquid and vapour coexist in equilibrium. For water: 0.01 °C and 0.00611 bar. F = 0 there.

quiz.q: Write the phase rule for a one-component system and give F for one, two and three phases.
quiz.a: F = C − P_ph + 2 = 3 − P_ph, where P_ph is the number of phases present. One phase F = 2, two phases F = 1, three phases F = 0.

quiz.q: Why is part of a P–V isotherm horizontal below T_c?
quiz.a: Because liquid and vapour coexist there. At a fixed T the saturation pressure is fixed, so P stays constant while V runs from v_f to v_g.

quiz.q: Why is the latent heat zero at the critical point?
quiz.a: Saturated liquid and saturated vapour become identical. There is no phase boundary to cross, so no heat is needed to change phase.

quiz.q: A sample of water is at 1 bar and 150 °C. How many degrees of freedom does it have, and what phase is it?
quiz.a: 150 °C is above the saturation temperature at 1 bar, which is about 100 °C, so the water is superheated vapour. One phase present, so F = 3 − 1 = 2: for a single phase of a pure fluid, T and P can be chosen independently.

quiz.q: A piston keeps water at 1 bar while it is heated from 25 °C to 120 °C. Give F at each stage and describe the heating curve.
quiz.a: At 25 °C: liquid, F = 2. At 100 °C boiling starts, F = 1, and the temperature stays at 100 °C while liquid turns into vapour. Above 100 °C: vapour, F = 2. On a temperature–enthalpy plot the middle stage is a flat plateau.

quiz.q: Water at 250 bar is cooled from 400 °C to 100 °C. Does it boil? Explain using the phase diagram.
quiz.a: No. 250 bar lies above P_c = 221 bar, so the constant-pressure path never crosses the vaporisation curve. Liquid and vapour never coexist: the fluid passes continuously from supercritical to a dense liquid, with no horizontal segment and no latent heat.

beyond: Not for the exam. Plant design uses equations of state fitted to a few measured saturation pressures and densities, not the ideal gas law, and process simulators carry dozens of them. Supercritical CO₂ power cycles, hydrogen storage and CO₂ pipelines all operate in the high-pressure region where the dome flattens.
